utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you deal with whether they were able to effectively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- extra governmental groups? Yes or no. If it's yes, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, local governments I do deal with. Local military units I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you deal with effective, the effective control, sir? Do you understand the term of art effective control? You've been here for seven and a half years. Where have you been? Do you understand that term? And that's the question the essence of the question is did they have effective control at the very local level? Yes, no, I don't know, I didn't examine it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a few different things you mentioned. First of all, if we're talking about municipal governments I can only answer insofar as I do in the report and cite the documents I do which I think shows --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a good level of control now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand you're not answering the question we'll move on. In your -- in your -- your research you examine those organs -- this is on paragraph 2 -- that you assume, my word, that you claim effectively exercise power. Okay. Now this is an assumption on your part you assume that they "effectively exercise power," are you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you read the next sentence, I explain what I mean by that. And what I mean is I'm talking about those organisations that actually functioned as opposed to temporary governments that were set up as parted of a peace programme but never got off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was there to preempt talking about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 3 you chose not to discuss the day-to-day workings of the military combat units. Should you not have at least discussed the relations of military units to local -- to the local civilian organs under discussion?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that not to be part of what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't -- you weren't interested in for instance if there was the effective chain -- the effectiveness of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay but -

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I did not think I was supposed on it making --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's not in your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- dealing with narrowly military subjects and I would consider that narrowly military subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Or the ability of the civil administrators to influence the military including the local militia. That's not in your report either?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the relationship, the de jure relationship between the military and the civilian structures is something which I do address. However, their ability to control what you call local militia, I think, was -- that's another thing I thought outside of the scope of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's not in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 4 you say that you used extensive -- that you -- "Extensive use of primary sources from one side of a conflict has advantages in disadvantages which need to be kept in mind focusing primarily on primary sources written by Herceg-Bosna organs and leaders during the period gives a very direct picture on what they thought and did at the time," and you go on. I take it you stand by that. That's a yes, no, or I --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- disagree with myself.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So here you were only interested in looking at one side of the -- the documents of only one side?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, and I will say with my no, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I finish my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I asked you whether you looked at one side and the answer was yes. I move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour that mischaracterises the record, because what Mr. Karnavas repeatedly does as he does here at line 17 and 18 is he gets an answer and then he restates the answer using different terminology. Mr. Tomljanovich, you can go through the past several pages of transcript, if you wish --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll listen to Mr. Tomljanovich rather than have to hear Mr. Scott who obviously -- I'll listen to Mr. Tomljanovich, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, he said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would ask, Your Honour, that Mr. Scott be told to sit down and allow me to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljanovich can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to not object when Mr. Karnavas mischaracterises the record so he comes back on line 15 and says: "So you were only interested." He didn't ask him what he was interested in, he asked him what he looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not fair to the witness to say: "You weren't interested in this." That's not what Mr. Tomljanovich said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can answer the question that's fine. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you should not mischaracterise the questions or -- but please, put your question again so that we can follow the answer of the.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Give us the reason why you only looked at one side, please keep it under two minutes, how about that? And I would appreciate if Mr. Scott would quit making remarks, you know. I can tolerate a certain degree of his obnoxiousness but I think he's going beyond the pale at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please answer the question. Question that you can read at line 23 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I intended on looking at what -- how Herceg-Bosna structures and organs and what it is they did. Now, what I was saying in the paragraph you cited was that what I wanted to do is take the primary source documents which they themselves produced not quite exclusively but very heavily their documents as a description of what they're doing. Before I did that, I gave the Judges and everyone in the trial the warning that when I'm doing this you have to understand that I'm drawing from their own account of things and when you see my cite their documents, I'm citing from their account of things and that's what has to be remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was the reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just an example. There's something I found extremely interesting in your report in relation with the establishment of tribunals and Judges appointed by Herceg-Bosna. You deal with this subject. So in line with Mr. Karnavas's question, I'd like to know the following: As an expert did you wonder whether they decided to appoint a new prosecutor, new judges, set up new courts? Was it because the judges or the prosecutors or the courts of Bosnia and Herzegovina were not functioning? Was it the reason why they appointed new ones, or was it because -- was it for other reasons these institutions were working but for some other reasons they decided to appoint new judges, prosecutors and tribunals? I believe that this is a very interesting question. What do you have to say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think it's an interesting question as well and I think the answer to Your Honour's question comes from and I forget the date but I do cite it in report the meeting of the HVO HZ HB in October of 1992 when they discuss the law on courts. They were presented with two options and two draft laws. One had the advantage of being acceptable to the existing authorities of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the other option had the advantage of giving them control and bringing the judicial organs more in line with the other organs which they created. And they chose to pick the version which gave them the greatest freedom of action and which was the most different from the system which preceded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that they adopted a new legal system, a new criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What are you suggesting here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they're discussing I think it's actually now the specifics -I can't tell you off the top of my head - but in October of 1992 when they discuss I believe it's the decree on the courts, they talk about setting up a new structure, and there's two proposals and this is the proposal which is the most novel and the most different from that which existed, yes. Now, criminal procedure is another thing, and the Criminal Code is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they adopt a new criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- well, the Criminal Code, they adopt the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as long as it's not in contradiction with their own ordinances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. By the way, did they appoint new judges in October? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They set up the new structures. Now, as far as judicial appointments --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When you say new structures, explain that to us because you're the expert. When you say new structures, explain this in detail because this is something that you obviously went into and you claim to have some knowledge, so please tell us what structures are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I mean, if you don't remember or you don't know just say so and I'll move along?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately without my report I can't quote you chapter and verse on the decree they reached. All I can tell you is that when they were confronted with two options at the meeting of the HVO HZ HB --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- They chose the one which was the most novel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Main may I just come back to the question just asked, Mr. Karnavas but did not get an answer and it was about criminal procedure. You only got an answer about criminal law and I would like to hear the answer about criminal procedure that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that would be nice, presupposing that the gentleman read the criminal procedure and compared the two but that would be nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by criminal procedure. All I've seen is that the criminal code and the law on misdemeanours was adopted, the existing BiH and SFRJ laws were adopted and taken over I think in some case was amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You know the difference between criminal procedure and substantive criminal law? If you don't know, say I don't know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as well as a lawyer does, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the answer is you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could guess, but no point in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe Judge Trechsel that may answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you ignore the constitutional and legal basis which imposed the obligation citizens, towns, municipalities, communities to defend their country; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in this particular well, depends what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we're going to get to that. That's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, did I cite the law on defence of BiH no I did not cite it but I did look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you say the law on defence of BiH, which law are we talking about are we talking about the All People's Defence or the law on armed forces of BiH? What is it that you're talking about? And incidentally I think it should be the SRBiH; right? The socialist republic of BiH at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to take our break. Yes. It's unfortunate, Mr. President, but we'll get back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is ten to 4.00. We reconvene at 4.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We left off, Mr. Tomljanovich, when I asked you about whether you had looked at the constitutional and legal basis which impose the obligation on the citizens, towns, municipalities, and communities to defend their country, and I wasn't sure that you had answered that question. So --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it on? Is it on? Yes, now it's on. Thank you. Thanks. I looked at the constitutional and legal basis for the obligations of towns, cities, municipalities in -- within the HVO Herceg- Bosna system. As far as the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, I briefly looked at the law on defence, but I considered that to be outside of the scope of what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me say -- let me ask you this: You say within the HVO Herceg-Bosna system. Let's -- let's backtrack. Before there was Herceg-Bosna, there was the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And actually while there was Herceg-Bosna as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, but we're going to go step-by-step. And that was just -- and before Bosnia and Herzegovina got its independence, it was part of Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, under the two -- both the -- the federal constitution and the constitution for the republic, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they not provide for -- or make it obligatory for citizens, towns and municipalities, cities to defend the town in case of need?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had the concept of All People's Defence, that all people would be mobilised in the event of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we're going to get to that. Now, I take it when you said that you looked at -- well, you qualified your answer that you just looked at the HVO -- the Herceg-Bosna system. Did you look at the constitution, the then existing constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to see what exactly was inside that legal instrument with respect to municipalities being able to organise themselves in case of a --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: An emergency. You looked at that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at that and it's precisely the things you're talking about. I just briefly looked at the existing constitution in regards to communities and municipalities just for my own background because that's a issue that's going to be coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You agree with me if we're going to look at the establishment of the HZ HB where municipalities are organising themselves, keeping in mind of course the events that are unfolding at the time, one would have to look at it within the scope of the constitution of the republic, right, or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No insofar as I did not consider it was my role to be deciding whether or not what they did was in fact constitutional and whether it was an allowed association of municipalities because that's a value judgement beyond what I thought I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me make sure I understand this correctly, and so as I -- as I stand here asking you these questions, it is your position that you are unable as an expert witness to give an opinion with respect to whether the HZ HB, HR HB was constitutional or not, was within the -- was, yeah, constitutional or not was within the then constitution for Bosnia- Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was my role to provide a definitive answer. Just to mention who thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who reached which conclusions at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, let's assume that you're doing your oral exams for your Ph.D. and your professor wants you to answer the questions directly.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't ask you what your role was. From your previous answer, it would appear that what -- you're making an admission here that you do not know whether HZ HB, HR HB was constitutional or not; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that the Constitutional Court thought it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand what the Constitutional Court -- and we're going to get there, but as you stand here today, because you were asked to look at the construct, how it was established, and I would imagine that in trying to determine how it was established one would have to look at where it was established, in what confines, and of course the circumstances, but in trying to determine how it was established, did you look at the then existing constitution and try to make a determination whether it was permissible for these municipalities under those circumstances to organise -- to organise themselves? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that would be a value judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Now, let's assume that you were asked to do that. It would be fair to say that given that, you have no legal training, by your own admission, and I think it was Ms. Alaburic that more or less walked you through some documents to show how you're actually incapable of even understanding and knowing how to read the law. It would be fair to say that if that had been your mission, you would not be able to fulfil it, given your background?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it wasn't his mission, what's the relevance of the question? He wasn't qualified to do something he didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because I dare say, Your Honour -- first I would like to have answer to my question and then I will state the obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How -- it's pure speculation, hypothetical, don't exist in the real world. Are you qualified to do something you didn't do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all events, I understood the gist of the question, and it enters into the Defence case theory. Now, the question is the following that the Defence is asking you: On the basis of studies, documents, research, context, everything that you had available, the inhabitants of the municipality, did they have the power to defend themselves, to set up a unity, military or otherwise, and entity, in order to stand up to a potential aggressor? The documents, the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or texts from ex-Yugoslavia, did they provide for the inhabitants to do that, to constitute some sort of entity, unity, paramilitary, paralegal, legal, or whatever, in your opinion? You studied the question. You examined it. Because it goes to the heart of the matter, to the heart of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I could answer Your Honour's question, there's really two parts to that. First of all, as far as the Defence obligation of persons under the constitution, all persons had a duty to defend the existing order and the existing constitution. Now, the question of associations of municipalities is a separate question, and the associations of municipalities are supposed to be done for an economic, not a defence -- not for the purposes of defence, as far as I understand. So that's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If I may continue, Mr. President. First of all, let's go back a little bit. First, you told us that you didn't -- that you're not competent to thoroughly read and understand legal instruments such as a constitution; correct? You don't have the legal background or the training.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, and I'm not worried because that because there's no shortage of lawyers in the room today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I didn't ask you about the shortage of lawyers. Now, sir, my question was whether you were competent to give us an opinion on whether it was legal or not legal, and you said that that's - - that you were not asked to do that; correct? Am I to understand that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not asked to do that but that's a separate question from my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to get there step-by-step. Had you been asked, let's just say that for the sake of context it would have been necessary for you to make that determination, would it be fair to say based on your previous answers that you would not have been able to fill that part of your mandate because you lack the necessary legal qualifications; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never -- I've -- I have always maintained I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said -- but yet you just stated here, and you just gave a legal opinion to Their Honours that based on your reading of the constitution that they could only -- the municipalities could only gather in -- they could only form associations for economic purposes. Is it your opinion, then, that based on your reading of the constitution and you were reading of the All People's Defence, and your reading of other legal instruments which by the way you've stated you're not competent to do so, but is it your opinion these legal instruments do not provide for municipalities to associate themselves in times of need such as where there is a war?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object to Mr. Scott trying to one, interfere; and two, trying to give witness clues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going -- I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object if the questions are improper and the characterisation is improper. What this witness has never said and this is why - and I'm sorry, I tried to come back in here and not get on my feet and I hope not to, but I'm not going to allow Mr. Karnavas to mischaracterise the testimony of this witness. Mr. Tomljanovich has never said he's not competent to answer these particular questions. He said he's not a lawyer. Now, that is not an end to the inquiry. He may be a trained expert in other areas which allows him to read certain historical documents and state an opinion. So if he says, I'm not a lawyer, that's not the same as Mr. Karnavas saying you've admitted you're not competent. They're not the same thing and I will not allow Mr. Karnavas to mischaracterise the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Tomljanovich, you've said you're not lawyer. We've known that ever since you entered the courtroom. But what we know as Judges is you're a historian and if a historian broaches the history of a country he has to start out and proceed by doing historical research and also deal with problems that are not strictly within the area of expertise that he deals with but that are related, structures, power relations, the army, and the various basic texts, constitutions, laws, rules and regulations, things of that kind. So in your work as a historian, because it's not your work as a lawyer that you're asked about now, but as an historian, did you ask yourself these questions? Did you ask about Territorial Defence matters, defence by individuals faced with an aggression from outside, an external aggression, things of that kind? Did you review those subjects? It's like the secessionist war in the United States, for example. You wouldn't have to be a lawyer. Would he not look at all the legal aspects of the problems at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should answer that in a little bit more detail. First of all, I did look at all of those matters, and I've dealt with them in previous trials and in other documents, but in a, you know, rather superficial way. I didn't deal with them specifically for this report because it was my understanding that no one was -- this trial wasn't about whether or not those particular -- whether or not the HVO and its foundation itself was legal. I didn't offer any opinion on that, and I didn't think there was any point to do so. If that does become an issue, I think I've used the documents which would lead the Judges to where you'd have to go to make that decision, but that's certainly -- something in that detail is not something I've looked at, although I do have my own opinion as to what their motivations were and what was allowed under the existing law on constitution, which is not an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may. May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, continue, Mr. Karnavas. But what we know is the witness is not a lawyer but an historian. Bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of 19th century history, by the way, Croatian history, who has taught some survey courses in other periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir -- sir, I take it if I were to walk you through the constitution, the 1974 constitution, or the law on the All People's Defence, it wouldn't make much of -- it would be sort of an exercise in futility since you're not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be entirely up to you and what it is you intend to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you look at the law on All People's Defence which was, incidentally in the Official Gazette of the socialist republic of BiH? And I'm sure your office would have had it. Did you look at it and study it to see to what extent it provided for the citizens at the very local level moving up to the municipalities and further on up to the state level to organise themselves in case of war? Did you study is that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a very long time ago, but it's generally known that in the system of the former Yugoslavia everyone had a defence obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. When we talk about everyone, municipalities also had obligations, did they not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they had to have a defence plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They had to have a defence plan. Okay. And you would agree with me at least during that period of time it would have been necessary for municipalities to at least on an individual basis to organise themselves within the municipality to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I wouldn't make any representations as to what was the role of the municipality and what was the role of the central organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking that. But they do have some role?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do have some role, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want to get drawn back into this argument but from listening to you last time with the central bank not functioning and there being no currency, the state as it was such as it was back in 1992 could not -- was not providing funds at the local level for, say, military purposes. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say anything about that with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you look into it to see whether, at the local level, these folks could rely on the state government, whether it be for military protection or for weapons, for salaries, et cetera? Did you look into that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you look at any of the municipalities, incidentally I know that you were told to focus, I know only on HVO, only on the Croats, but did you by any chance look to make a comparison if anywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina, say in Tuzla or other municipalities, whether they organised themselves and whether they did anything to make sure that they could provide the day-to-day needs for their citizens, needs that were not being provided, services which were not being provided by the state government as it was required to do so under normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you said something about -- and it just caught my ear little bit, about -- you said you weren't -- your mission wasn't there to talk about the legality or illegality of the HZ HB. That was left to somebody else. But if we look at your report, you talk about de jure and de facto, and I have to tell you that outside legal terms, you know, legal -- a legal atmosphere, people don't go around talking about de jure and de facto. What is your definition of de jure and what is your definition of de facto so we know that you as a non-lawyer what your definition is, and I can proceed on my question?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: De jure is how things function according to the law; de facto is how things in fact do function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can agree on that. I think we can accept that definition. Now if you're not there to make a determination on whether something is legal or illegal, unconstitutional or constitutional, you not being a lawyer by your own admission, how can you then -- and then as you've indicated you weren't asked to look into it, it wasn't part of your mandate, how then can you put into your report a section on the de jure aspect?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had access to the official Gazettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incidentally, and I take it that's what you looked at official Gazettes and the minutes of the meetings, of the various meetings.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And other documents that we had access to as well but most -- most of the legislation we know about is in the official Gazettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it you were also looking at the legislation from the state level as well to see whether -- I know we talked a little bit about the Constitutional Court decision and we're going to get to that, but did you look at the other legislation or did you just focus on the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say state level or BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I made a deliberate decision not to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay but nonetheless it is your expert opinion when you talk about de jure it's simply based on looking at these documents?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when say de jure, at least if I understand your definition of de jure, and the scope of your report within this definition, your analysis is what -- you know, how the law -- you know, if we read it, analyse, it synthesise it, we come up with this de jure analysis that you have come which doesn't mean that it's constitutional or unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay. Now, you said you looked at it. Then there's a section de facto, and again I need to pin you down a little bit, because earlier on I asked you a question about whether you had looked into to what extent, to what extent the top leaders, as you put it, had actual effective command and control or effective control over at the very local level, and as I understand it, what you said was you didn't look into that; right? You're shaking your head?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does that mean you did look into it and I'm wrong or you did look at it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked into it only as documents permitted. There is documentation that I cited in this report of the municipalities and their relationship with the central Herceg-Bosna government but only insofar as documentation allowed me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. All right. Well, I'm not going to go through the 1974 BiH constitution or the law on All People's Defence. We'll save that for someone else. But suffice it to say in looking at your report, I don't see you articulating anywhere or citing anywhere in any concrete fashion the law on All People's Defence. So may I conclude that at least for the analysis of this report, which you say is balanced and complete and what have you, the law on All People's Defence was not considered, hence why it's not in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I considered the previous law on All People's Defence to be superseded by the HVO decree on the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, you say superseded now. Help me out here because you're throwing me off on that one. Are you saying that law was above or below, which one?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the thinking of the persons who applied the law judging -- the inference I make, judging on the fact that BiH laws had to be adopted especially by the HZ HB to be put into effect it's my assumption that their law would have priority unless the existing law had already been an adopted, otherwise there wouldn't be any point to adopt existing BiH law such as they did with the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me cut this Gordian knot. As I understand it, and maybe you can agree with me, what you're saying is that state law, and that the constitution is above all other laws; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: N, but I'm just -- I'm going to walk you through it so help me out here work with me. Is it not your understanding that the highest law in the state would have been the constitution?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the republican constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, we're talking about socialist republic of BiH.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have much of a personal opinion. I just know that it's not something which was thought as the highest law in the land by people in the HVO during most of the period in which they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you think the HVO did. I'm asking you on a theoretical basis. Now you can tell me, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a theoretical basis it sounds plausible that the republican constitution should take precedence over Republika Srpska law and Herceg- Bosna law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And on a theoretical basis would it also sound plausible to you that the law on All People's Defence, which is at the state level, would also apply, those principles would also apply?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not within the HVO HZ HB system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Step-by-step I said. On a theoretical basis, because at this point in time you told us that you don't know whether HVO HZ HB is constitutional or not. Okay? And I'm asking you a very concrete question. Is the legislation coming from the state such as the All People's Defence above legislation, above legislation that is being put at the municipal level? Leaving out HZ HB. Yes, no, I don't know? Those -- you know.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think you misrepresented one of the things I said earlier. I didn't say I didn't know whether it was constitutional or not, I just said that wasn't a decision for me to make and that I could only point to the institutions that did declare it unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But hold it, hold it, hold it. I'm going to stop you right there because you're now like a back slider, because I thought we established that. You're not a constitutional expert, didn't really consult the constitution, didn't consult lawyers that would be able to help you out. You said it wasn't part your mandate, so now are you saying that it was not constitutional? Are you forming an opinion at this point in time? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, because the objection is Mr. Karnavas is once again mischaracterising once again what the witness said he doesn't say to say what his opinion was. He cited the two Constitutional Court decisions of the Bosnia Constitutional Court that said both the Croatian Community and Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna were unconstitutional. He don't have to be a lawyer to report as a historian of the Constitutional Court rule. And that's what his testimony has been and again Mr. Karnavas mischaracterises it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you called here as an expert as an historian on 19th century history or are you here to give us an opinion on the legal constructs as you put it de jure and de facto of the HZ HB that existed within the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my understanding that I'm not supposed to do either. It's my understanding that I'm supposed to point the Judges to the evidence that's relevant to understanding the governing structures and processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at one point you liken the HZ HB to the Republika Srpska, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you please point where in your report do you make a detailed analysis for the Trial Chamber to make a determination because you're just -- you make that statement, but I see no analysis, and don't tell me what you learned in other cases because I'm talking about this report. Is there an analysis in the report? Yes, no, or maybe you forgot to put it or you ran out of pages or something you were told to take it out. I don't know. What is the answer?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll used the -- you used the folksy metaphor that if it walks like a duck and it talks like a duck, it's a duck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where's the analysis, sir? A concrete analysis. Let's assume that the Judges have no idea what the RS Republika Srpska is and I cannot make assumption that our Honourable Chamber knows that. Where in your report do you make an analysis so at least when we look at the two we can say uh-huh, they must be the same?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given that the Republika Srpska was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, sir I'm asking you for your report. I am entitled to notice, I got notice of your report. I'm asking where in your report you make the comparison, the analytical comparison other than merely making a statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided a copy of his report and be allowed to look at pages 8, 9 and 10, please. He doesn't even have his report in front of him. So perhaps if the report could be provided and his attention could be directed to pages 8, 9, 10 and 11 of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although I believe I could answer that question without looking at my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could have two sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think it was necessary to do so because in my opinion it was obvious that an association of municipalities put together stated for the benefit of one particular ethnic group by the political party of one particular ethnic group was a very similar thing, and I thought -- I didn't think I needed to go through every point in which they're similar in order for that to be quite obvious to everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or dissimilar.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some ways they may be dissimilar as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's -- since we talked about this constitutional court decision, maybe we could go through that, but just incidentally before we get to that decision, might I ask if you looked at all the documents that were referenced when we had Mr. Kljuic here as a witness showing that the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina were continually asking the state, asking the government in Sarajevo to take measures because of the imminent threat. And I'm referring to -- we have at least seven documents that were presented. You indicated you saw Mr. Kljuic when he was testifying. You watched that portion. Might I ask whether you looked at those documents? And I can cite them out. Would you like me to cite them out?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you cite them or not, it's entirely up to you, but I can tell you from -- at the beginning I didn't see more than about an hour's of Mr. Kljuic's cross-examination in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you consider -- did you consider P 00032, the meeting of the Presidency of the HDZ BiH 4 April 1991, it's been introduced. Did you look at it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure although that document probably came up during Mr. Kljuic's testimony in Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They all did I'm just asking you whether you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it did in Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In Kordic you were in court, as I understand?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A fact that you omitted last time you were asked. You were actually in court and I point that out to the record to further demonstrate how closely intertwined he is in the Prosecution team. What about P 00034, the second meeting of the Presidency HDZ BiH 16 April 1991? Did you consider that in your report because I don't see it anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically for this report I probably looked at all the meetings of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about P 00041, the sixth regular meeting of the Presidency of HDZ BiH 10 July 1991? These are all incidentally meetings where the same topic is coming up, the imminent threat of danger, the state should be doing something let's organise ourselves did you look at that for your report?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not because I assumed Mr. Kljuic, as a live witness would deal with these.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you say you assume. How did you know I was going to introduce these documents because they didn't come in, even though they have a P number, I was the one who showed them to Mr. Kljuic or many of them how could you make such an assumption?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just guessing based on what happened in Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Okay. So you're clairvoyant as well. Okay. Well what P 00042, the HDZ BiH meeting in Busovaca with the HDZ BiH Presidency and this is 21 July 1991. That's not in your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Or P 00047, the second ordinary session of the Main Board of the HDZ in Prozor Rama, 6 August 1992, that's not in there either, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then there are two more documents that's the 9th regular session which is P 00052 and P 0051 is the press release from the 9th regular session and respectively they are both 26 August 1991. That wasn't in your report, and that wasn't considered; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it wasn't considered because all these meetings of the party are things that I have seen a number of times before and I deliberately didn't think it was necessary to put them in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But -- okay. If the -- if the Croats are alarmed that there's a war going on in Croatia, that the -- that the JNA is using Bosnian territory to attack Croatia and that the state government, the Sarajevo government is unable or incapable or unwilling to do anything, okay, do you think that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be alarmed to the extent that they might look at the All People's Defence in organising themselves at least for the purposes of fending off an imminent threat of danger? Did you that I can that into consideration?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Beyond the scope of the report, Your Honour. Again he wasn't here to speculate as to whether it was right or wrong for what the Croats did what they did but simply to testify as to the structures and processes that were established, whether they were good or bad, evil or good, whatever they were, Mr. Tomljanovich has said not to express value judgements but simply to report the structures as think existed. And that's all he's done. And again Mr. Karnavas wants to talk -- have this witness talk everything about the Defence case which has nothing to do with this what witness was asked to do. Mr. Karnavas can call his own expert, he can call his own witnesses until as long as the Court wants to give him the time to do that but not to ask this witness to do beyond the scope of what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I indicated, Mr. President, because there are value judgements in the report, because there are conclusions, it begs these sorts of questions. Now, to suggest that I can call my own expert, well, let me put it -- frankly, I don't have seven years to hire somebody for this kind of money that he's getting paid number one. And number two, that I -- the burden is -- the burden of proof is on the Prosecution, and that's why I'm entitled to go into this. So if the Prosecution is putting forward a report with conclusions, I'm entitled to challenge them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, let's go look at the constitutional decision, and -- because that's something that you do cite, okay? That's something that you do cite. And do you recall the date by any chance?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been in mid many of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's 18 September, 1992. Now, before we get there, before we get there, work with me a little bit here, I want to look at one document, and that's 339. I guess it's -- it's P 00339. This is, as you may recall while we're waiting to get it up, this is agreement on friendship and cooperation, okay?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, to those who don't know too much about this, this is an agreement between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in fact, it was an agreement struck between Tudjman, who was -- Franjo Tudjman, who was the president, then president of the Republic of Croatia, and Izetbegovic who was the president of the Presidency, not the president of the country but the president of Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it and I doesn't know if this is in the record yet, but I would certainly ask and invite the close scrutiny and attention of the Trial Chamber in reading this agreement to also keep in mind Prosecution Exhibit P 00336. This is a presidential transcript that was on 21 July 1992. I will not be going into it, but this is the transcript of the meeting between President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic, and at the conclusion of this transcript, which is, as you can see, very thick, this agreement is reached, but it talks about -- it has the dynamics particularly with respect to certain language that I wish to highlight here today. So I just put that for the record. Now, sir, if we look at item number 1, this would be on page 2 of this agreement, and the ERN 00810568. It says that they have agreed as follows: The president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the president of the Republic of Croatia have agreed that the future state system of Bosnia and Herzegovina will proceed from the principle of full equality of the three constituent nations, Muslim, Croat, and Serbs. The constitutional political system of the country will be based on constituent units in the establishment of which due account will be taken of national, historical, cultural, economic, traffic, and other elements. You saw that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incidentally, I don't mean to -- I should ding you up a little bit for sloppiness in your report. At one point you talk about ethnic groups, and I believe it -- it kind of struck me odd that you would use that term. I believe it was on page 4. Hold on. Let me look at it for a second. I've got so much -- this is at paragraph 9. You use the term ethnic, and you of all people, and I think I can use that in such a tone that you should know better these are historical nations the Muslims and Serbs, they're not ethnic groups; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's only if you make the distinction between ethnic groups and nations. I didn't go back into defining the terms. If you want to go --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, you got your Ph.D. from Yale; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I understand -- you're probably wondering why is that important. I understand that your mentor or one of them was Ivo Banac; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And he's written pretty much the definitive book, I mean the seminal book on nationalities; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nationalities in the former Yugoslavia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. And I take it since you were studying 19th century Croatian history and since he was your mentor, you might have read his book, it might have been helpful because for nothing else, for brownie points, that you're reading your professor's books; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read his books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, he talks about the historical nations these are not ethnic groups. These are nations these are not ethnic groups in the sense of what we know in the United States or other countries.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a distinction Professor Banac makes and I can tell you what he means when he makes that distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina are an ethnic group and not a historical nation; is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's my understanding they're both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on. In any event, go back to the document on the agreement, here they're talking about three constituent nations. By the way, was that not in the constitution, the then-existing constitution in Bosnia-Herzegovina describing them as three constituent nations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's frequently cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's frequently cited and also in the all the negotiations that preceded that, it was always maintained that the constitution recognised three constituent peoples; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and what exactly that meant was the root of a lot of disagreement between them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When you say between them, between whom?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leaders of the Serbs, the leaders of the Muslims, and the leaders of the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just touch on that a little. That's almost too good to let go. Are you suggesting by any chance that during any of these negotiations the Croats who were negotiating for the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina had a dilemma as to what constituted a -- a Bosnian Muslim who are now called Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what you call a dilemma.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did they express -- did they ever say, no, he's not -- the Muslims are not a constituent nation? Did they ever say? That's a broad enough question, let alone who is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't -- well, they didn't, as far as I know, question that constitutional point, although they did question the nationality and the nationhood of Bosnian Muslims rather frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is it not a fact that on every single peace agreement which was proposed and which the Croats signed, that all of them called for and recognised the Muslim people of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a constituent nation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not positive but in official documents that would have been the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that's what they're signing. Haven't you read any of these documents?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read quite a few of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now let's -- if we can go to item 6. Item 6, and this is on page -- with the ERN number 00810569. It says here the armed component of the Croatian - "The armed component of the Croatian Defence Council is an integral part of the united armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian Defence Council will have us represent in the Joint Command, in the Joint Command, of the armed forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in this agreement, HVO, the military component, is recognised officially, is it not, in the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but conditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it's recognised, is it not? And this is July 21, 1992. We are going to go on. Now, it says provisional civil authorities, let me underscore that, "Provisional civil authorities established in wartime conditions within the scope of the Croatian Defence Council will be made to conform as soon as possible with the constitutional judicial system of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in talks pertaining to this matter," and talks pertaining to this matter, "will be initiated immediately in the principles stated in point 1 of this agreement." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at this point in time, sir, was there a commission or were they planning to form a commission to draft a new constitution for Bosnia- Herzegovina, for the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you not recall?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But at some point there was, was there not? If you don't know, say I don't know?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at different times there were, but when exactly, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say different times, I'm not asking you 1994 and I'm not asking you 1995. I'm asking you 1992 now?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember if they had a commission in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it says on point 7 and I think this might be important in light of our last guest that was here, our last witness: "The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia will reciprocally allow their citizens to acquire dual citizenship." I highlight that for the Court's attention since that is the contested issue at times. Now, this, sir, was signed on July 21, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I cited to a presidential transcript. I take it you read that transcript of that particular day and know pretty much the ongoings and negotiations especially where they laboured, and I don't use that word lightly over paragraph one which we read?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now if we look at P 00346. This is dated July 26, 1992, and if we look at it, this is a letter that is sent, if we look at it, from the general secretary of the HDZ BH. Now, pay close attention to the very first line. It says: "On July 23, 1992, the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia-Herzegovina received a letter from the Constitutional Court dated 22 July, 1992." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here is what I'm trying to point out. That a day -- a day after Izetbegovic signs an agreement, it appears that someone in his government moves the Constitutional Court to begin proceedings against the HDZ, the HZ HB, and the HVO, the very same organisations which under the friendship agreement he recognises?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Karnavas can tell us how those two things are inconsistent since that is what he implies because there is no inconsistency between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the inconsistency is as follows: You have the president of the Presidency, who presumably, we have to believe and trust the previous Prosecution witness, Galbraith, who was talking for the entire country he signs the agreement. In the agreement, he recognises the HVO and also if we look at paragraph 6 of the provisional agreement, the second part, it says provisional civil authorities. What were the provisional civil authorities? If we look at all of the headings of the -- all of the headings of the -- of the HZ HB and of the HVO, the civilian component; first of all it's part of the HVO and second of all it talks about provisionality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could answer that question if I may. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all -- first of all, would you agree that this is the day after the agreement?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's -- well, yes, the 22nd would be the day after, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and I take it you don't see a contradiction in that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I can tell you why not if you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're not going to speculate, are you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you're going to cite something to me, something I can look at?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Go for it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't want you to tell me what you believe. I want you to tell me what you know. Cite me a document that says that -- that explains how is it that on one day Izetbegovic is signing an agreement after a full day's session and the next day you got the Constitutional Court trying to say that these institutions are illegal.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple. First of all and then I'll get to the document as I remember it, first of all, there's the separation of powers within Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Constitutional Court could review a matter without --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me -- okay. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Before you go any further. You said separation of powers. That's something we know the United States and something I studied a little bit about when I was studying constitutional law, but you've told us you're not a lawyer. You've told us you're not familiar with these legal instruments. On what basis, on what basis, what legal basis are you stating that there was separation of power especially, especially by this point in time, as I understand it, there had been a declaration of imminent threat of war, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know for sure as you sit here that there is, in fact, separation of power at this point in time in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Because if you don't, we're going to stop and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. I have a technical problem. The two documents we see: On the left a document in English and on the right a document in B/C/S. I wonder whether they are really the same documents, because you have been insisting that this document was a day from -- from a day after the agreement, and the English document, the agreement was 21st of July, I seem to recall you said, and I read that on 23rd --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you if you keep on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- they received -- it very well cannot be a letter of the next day if it speaks of another letter that is two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just read the whole text in English. It says: "On the 23 July, 1992, the Croatian Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina received a letter from the Constitution Court." So they received it on the 23rd and all these have a number of 22 July 1992. We don't have the letter. But they're making a reference to this. This is -- you know, so we have -- I'm trying to -- I guess you're using circumstantial evidence if you've got the agreement on the 21. They're saying we received the letter on the 23rd but that it was dated on the 22nd. It stands to follow that the next day they sent this -- they sent the letter out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me, and I take it at some point you read the decision that was on 18 September, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And by the way, getting back to the separation of power issue and I don't want to prolong it, but you really are unable at this point in time to tell us with any degree of legal certainty that there was separation of powers at that time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you with a fairly good degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Legal certainty?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with legal certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That this procedure was initiated by the Court itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you whether there was separation of power. I know the court could initiate it Izetbegovic can pick up the fop and ask the president of the Constitutional Court to institute proceedings. You don't know that. So I'm asking you, do you know for sure that the law as it existed at that point in time, okay, keeping in mind that you have a state of war, that you had separation of powers, yes or no, because you mentioned it, I didn't?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned it in the context of there being a contradiction between the Court initiating a procedure and Izetbegovic having said something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's a guess on your part.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a guess. I don't know if Izetbegovic had any influence over the court. The only thing know with certainty is the Court said they initiated themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now you said, "They said that." Who said that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Said it who, where, in the document or they told that to you personally?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's either -- and I should mention too that this particular document you have here and a number others --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, stick with me on the separation of powers issue because now you're making an assertion, and at some point the Trial Chamber is going to have a make a decision and I certainly would like to check it. Where is it that you know that there was separation of power in that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: De facto, I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: De jure point it out to me where?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You believe? Do you know for sure? Yes, no, I don't know, I'm taking a wild guess?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could look at another document, and this is P 00817, and I think this is relevant. The periods are relevant, Mr. President and Your Honours, because it kind of puts things more into perspective if I can say that. You're familiar with this document. This is -- this is the document that was signed by the Prime Minister, Mr. Akmadzic; correct? And he's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document and I can tell you why I didn't include it in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You see, don't try to --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I am familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But here in November 27, 1992, there is a decision signed by the -- by the Prime Minister, and the decision, it says that it appoints and authorises Dr. Jadranko Prlic the president of the Croatian Defence Council, not the defunct or the one that is under the constitutional suspension or the alleged or presumed, but it says the Croatian Defence Council to present to the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it goes on to list various things. It appoints him for instance, number 1, as a member of the RBH government staff for the collection of items to help RBH population survive. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, now, just to make sure that I hit this nail through the bottom and it goes through, let me show you also Exhibit 1D 00898, because this is an Official Gazette. So we don't merely have some Croat who is on this government signing a document or a decision which we can then say is motivated by his ethnic or national background but here we have the Official Gazette of republic the BiH and in this official document, okay, around you would recognise it being from the Official Gazette or should recognise it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I'd have to correct an implication you made earlier. Mile Akmadzic is a Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oh, I he is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and who he is is essential to understanding these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hold on. Are you suggesting -- are you suggesting that somehow Mile Akmadzic who is in Sarajevo at this time; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he still was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was in Sarajevo at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he still was in November of '92. He leaves somewhere I think a little after that but I'm not positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And are you suggesting here, because this is why I had the second document, are you suggesting that this clever Croat was able to get a decision, to issue a decision and put the stamp on, and we all know that the stamp counts, and then somehow get that decision to the Official Gazette for mankind and God to see and no one took notice of it? Because if you have a document to show that this was repealed or this was cancelled or demonstrated that Akmadzic was acting outside his authorities, his legal authorities and without the approval of the Presidency of the RBiH, I would like to know where it is.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could give an answer but it would require me talking about closed-session testimony I've heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, it says here in this decision -- it doesn't refer to Akmadzic. He's the one who has to sign it. This official document says, the last line: "The government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina hereby issues the following." So it's not Akmadzic who is actually issuing the decision. It's the government and he's merely the signatory as is required that's what the Prime Minister does and he affixes the seal to it isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM TOMLJANOVICH [Resumed]
